Development of aerobic methane oxidation, denitrification coupled to 
methanogenesis (AMODM) in a microaerophilic expanded granular sludge 
blanket biofilm reactor 
Xin Zhou a,b,c,*, Gonglei Wang a,b, Daling Ge a,b, Zeyang Yin a,b 
a College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Taiyuan University of Technology, Taiyuan, 030024, China 
b Innovation Center for Postgraduate Education in Municipal Engineering of Shanxi Province, Taiyuan, 030024, China 
c National Engineering Laboratory for Advanced Municipal Wastewater Treatment and Reuse Technology, Key Laboratory of Beijing for Water Quality Science and Water 
Environment Recovery Engineering, Beijing University of Technology, Beijing, 100124, China   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
AMODM 
EGSBBR 
Methane 
Nitrogen removal 
Microbial mechanism 
A B S T R A C T   
The issue of enhancing nitrogen removal and managing dissolved methane emission in anaerobic treatment 
systems is a major bottleneck in its wider application to treat high-strength organic wastewater with nitrate. 
Herein, a novel aerobic methane oxidation, denitrification coupled to methanogenesis (AMODM) process was 
developed in a glucose-fed microaerobic expanded granular sludge blanket biofilm reactor (EGSBBR) through in- 
situ utilization of produced methane for nitrogen removal. The 162-day operation demonstrated that long-term 
treatment performance under the decreased COD/NO3
−-N (C/N) ratio from 66.7 to 10 and the optimal C/N ratio 
for completing AMODM was found to be 16.7. Microbial community analysis further evidenced that Methanothrix 
as key methanogen predominated in the sludge bed, while Methlogaea as aerobic methane oxidizer was mainly 
detected in the packing bed of the hybrid system. Meanwhile, some facultative heterotrophic and dissimilated 
nitrate-reduction (DNRA) genera also co-existed. The profiling of key functional genes further proved concurrent 
occurrence of methanogenesis, aerobic methane oxidation and denitrification. Furthermore, possible microbial 
mechanism on AMODM process was elucidated from the prospective of targeted species interaction within the 
reactor. This research provides a robust and environment-friendly alternative process treating nitrate-containing 
organic wastewater towards efficient nitrogen removal, low resource consumption, bioenergy recovery and 
greenhouse gas reduction.   
1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) known as an energy-positive biotech­
nology has been extensively applied for high-strength organic waste­
water treatment (Rajeshwari et al., 2000) due to its attractive benefits of 
no oxygen supply and biogas (gaseous methane; G-CH4) recovery. 
However, amounts of dissolved methane (D-CH4) still remains in AD 
effluent due to its supersaturation (up to 22–28 g CH4/m3; 25–35 ◦C) 
(Kim et al., 2010; Souza et al., 2011) and fails to separate and reuse from 
the liquid phase. Even worse, D-CH4 may escape into the atmosphere 
and cause a strong greenhouse effect (IPCC, 2013) if it subjects to 
stripping like aeration (Daelman et al., 2012). Another major problem in 
the widespread application of the AD process is the limitation in 
removing nitrogen, especially for nitrogen-containing carbonaceous 
wastewater. To overcome it, one effective strategy is the sequential 
treatment of anaerobic followed by aerobic treatment (Akizuki and 
Toda, 2018). As such, nitrogen and organics can be removed by simul­
taneous denitrification and methanogenesis (SDM) (Andalib et al., 
2011) through recycling nitrifying liquid back to the front AD reactor. 
Nevertheless, its nitrate removal is largely affected by the availability of 
organic matters, which are competed between methanogens and de­
nitrifiers. Moreover, D-CH4 emission is still unsolved in SDM process. 
Recently, aerobic methane oxidation (AMO) as a newly important 
pathway in global carbon and nitrogen cycles has been firstly discovered 
in wastewater treatment systems (Ho et al., 2013). Particularly, AMO 
means that methane is capable of being oxidized into methanol and 
other oxidative products, thus providing alternative carbon sources for 
enhanced denitrification, namely aerobic methane oxidation coupled to

denitrification (AME-D) (Zhu et al., 2016). Based on microbial findings 
and potential possibilities, CH4 in-situ generated from the AD process is 
expected to be directly utilized by AMO microorganisms to intensify 
nitrogen removal by means of the integration of SMD and AME-D into a 
single methanogenic reactor under microaerophilic condition. There­
fore, synchronous removals of organics, nitrogen and D-CH4 with partial 
recovery of G-CH4 can be realized via aerobic methane oxidation, 
denitrification coupled to methanogenesis (AMODM). As far as our 
knowledge, however, it has not been exploited yet so far. 
The main purpose of the present study is to investigate the feasibility 
of AMODM in an expanded granular sludge blanket biofilm reactor 
(EGSBBR) to treat nitrate-containing organic wastewater and to unravel 
possible microbial mechanisms of AMODM based on the identification 
of key functional bacteria and genes using 16S rDNA sequencing 
technique. 
2. Material and methods 
2.1. Reactor setup 
A lab-scale continuous up-flow EGSBBR system was set up in Fig. S1. 
The effective volume of the whole system was 17 L (1.9 m height and 
9.0 cm inner diameter) was composed of main body (9 L) and triphase 
separator (8 L). The main body included an expanded granular sludge 
bed (bottom) and a packing bed (upper) filled with 25% (v/v) sponge 
cubes (8 × 8 × 8 mm) as media. The separator was fixed at the reactor 
top to separate treated wastewater, precipitate the sludge and collect the 
biogas. The biogas flowrate was measured by an electronic gas flow- 
meter and treated effluent was discharged from the weir located at the 
separator. The whole system was controlled at 35 ± 1◦C by a heater for 
promoting mesophilic methanogenesis. 
2.2. Operation procedure 
The reactor was inoculated with the mixture at a 2:1 vol ratio of 
thickener sludge (MLSS: 15.76 g/L) and aerobic activated sludge (MLSS: 
7.47 g/L) from a municipal wastewater treatment plant in Jinzhong city, 
China. COD and NO3
−-N were added in the synthetic wastewater in the 
form of glucose, sodium nitrate, respectively. The alkalinity and phos­
phorus source were provided by NaHCO3 and KH2PO4 and 1 mL/L trace 
element solution (5 g EDTA, 2 g FeCl3⋅4H2O 0.2 g CoCl2⋅6H2O, 0.5 g 
MnCl2⋅4H2O, 0.03 mg CuCl2⋅2H2O; 0.05 g ZnCl2, 0.1 g Na2SeO3，0.05 g 
NiCl2⋅6H2O, 0.09 g Na2MoO4, 0.05 g H3BO4 per liter). 
To accelerate methanogenesis during anaerobic digestion, the micro- 
aerobic pretreatment as a preferred method was used (Montalvo et al., 
2006). In this study, low dissolved oxygen (DO) and oxidation-reduction 
potential (ORP) under the liquid level 20 cm of the triphase separator 
were maintained at 0.22 ± 0.02 mg/L and −340 ± 30 mv, respectively 
to ensure the co-cultivation of methanogens, denitrifiers and aerobic 
methanotrophs. The pre-aerated feeding was pumped into the bottom of 
the up-flow reactor at ascending liquid velocity of 1.2 m/h by a peri­
staltic pump with 100% internal recycling ratio. The hydraulic retention 
time (HRT) was set to 2 d and no sludge was discharged resulting in the 
mixed liquid volatile suspended solid (MLVSS) increased from initially 
8.2 g/L to finally 15.0 g/L during the experiment. During the start-up 
stage, the reactor was initially fed with high-strength organic simulate 
wastewater only with the influent COD of 2000 mg/L and the influent 
pH was maintained at 7.2 ± 0.1 to enrich methane-producing bacteria. 
After the 46-day start-up period, lots of biogas bubbles were visibly 
observed, denoting the completion of methanogenesis. And then a 
certain amount of NO3
−-N began to be added into the feed. To explore the 
feasibility of AMODM, five different operations at C/N ratio from 66.7 to 
10 by adjusting influent NO3
−-N concentration were carried out during 
the 162-day experiment, while COD was kept always constant, shown in 
Table 1. 
2.3. High-throughput sequencing 
The samples of activated sludge in the sludge bed and biofilm in the 
packing bed was collected and stored in the refrigerator at −20 ◦C on 
Day 116 (Phase Ⅳ). The microbial community were analyzed by the 
Illumina high-throughput sequencing platform based on 16 S rDNA by 
Sangon Botech Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China) according to our previous 
study (Zhou et al., 2018). Key functional genes were compared and 
estimated by the Kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) 
database (https://www.kegg.jp) (Zhou et al., 2020). 
2.4. Chemical analysis 
NH4
+-N, NO2
−-N, NO3
−-N and COD concentrations were measured by 
HACH Lange cuvette kits. TN was the sum of NH4
+-N and NOx
−-N. pH, DO 
and ORP were monitored by a portable analysis meter (WTW 3420, 
Germany). The CH4 and CO2 concentrations of the gas samples over the 
headspace were determined by a gas chromatograph (GC-4000A, China) 
equipped with flame ionization (FID) detector and thermal conductivity 
(TCD) detector, respectively. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Reactor performance 
To rapidly establish AMODM in a methanogenic system, the influent 
C/N ratio as a crucial process parameter was mainly investigated. Fig. 1 
shows the overall time-course performance of the reactor under different 
influent C/N ratios. As shown in Fig. 1a, steadily low effluent COD (39.5 
± 12.3 mg/L) with the corresponding COD removal efficiency of 98.1 ±
0.7% was obtained in the whole experiment. The biogas production and 
influent and effluent pH are present in Fig. 1b. From the chart, methane 
yield as high as 608 mLCH4/d or 35.7 mL CH4/(L⋅d) was achieved in the 
PhaseI, suggesting successful build-up of methanation at the influent 
organic loading rate (OLR) of 1.0 kg COD/(m3⋅d). Subsequently, only a 
bit decrease in methane production was observed when the nitrate was 
increasingly added in PhasesII-III. Up to 120 mg/L nitrate in Phase Ⅳ, 
the generation of methane lowered to 403 mLCH4/d or 23.7 mL CH4/ 
(L⋅d), which was nearly 2/3 of its maximum production. The rise of the 
effluent pH in Fig. 1b also implied the satisfactory methanogenesis 
performance owing to evident accumulation of alkalinity during the 
methanation metabolism. Afterward, the CH4 production sharply 
declined to below 200 mL/d or in Phase Ⅴ by decreasing C/N ratio to 10. 
As the nitrate was added, more organics would be transformed by 
denitrification into CO2 instead of CH4, resulting in the decline of 
methane yield.

As for nitrate removal, as high as 98.9% NO3
−-N removal rate was 
accomplished in the whole operation in Fig. 1c. In comparison with 
stably complete NO3
−-N removal, however, average TN removal under­
went a gradual decrease from 87.7% to 71.2% as NO3
−-N increasing in 
the first three stages. But surprisingly, the nitrogen removal capability in 
Phase Ⅳ stopped falling but improved to 82.7% on the average instead. 
Taking decreased CH4 and increased CO2 production (in Fig. 1b) into 
consideration, methane oxidation might have play a significant role in 
unexpected improvement of TN removal. Under the microaerobic con­
dition, methane was firstly oxidized into methanol by aerobic methane- 
oxidizing bacteria, which was thrived in stable methane-producing and 
nitrate-rich environment and then reduced nitrate to nitrogen gas uti­
lizing oxidation products of methane as alternative carbon source for 
denitrification. 
Nevertheless, it was noted that TN removal efficiency significantly 
decreased and then stabilized up to nearly 75% if influent NO3
−-N further 
increased to 200 mg/L in Fig. 1c. In terms of sharp decline in methane 
generation and TN removal, methanogenesis was greatly inhibited and 
even deteriorated due to the low C/N ratio. Andalib et al. (2011) also 
found that methanogenesis would lose the competition with denitrifi­
cation if the C/N ratio dropped to below 10 in the SDM process. Like­
wise, the denitrification gradually dominated in nitrogen removal in 
ours study, as more nitrates were served as electronic acceptor for 
denitrification. That was why TN removal was recovered somewhat in 
the late period of Phase Ⅴ. During the operation, effluent TN was almost 
present in the form of NH4
+-N, indicating dissimilatory nitrate reduction 
to ammonia (DNRA) possibly involved in the nitrogen conversion. 
Andalib (Andalib et al., 2011) also reported the occurrence of DNRA 
during organic wastewater treatment at the presence of methane and 
nitrate. Overall, AMODM was successfully accomplished through 
adjusting C/N ratio via the coupling of methanogenesis, methane 
oxidation and denitrification in the single methanogenic reactor. 
3.2. Analysis of functional bacteria and key genes 
High-throughput sequencing was conducted to further identify the 
microbial community and associated genes on Day 116 in Phase Ⅳ. 
Fig. 2a depicts the major microbial community (abundance >0.5%) at 
the genus level in both the sludge and biofilm. According to the analysis, 
heterotrophic microorganisms including anaerobic/facultative bacteria 
(Saccharibacteria_genera_incertae_sedis, Smithella, Trichococcus, Thermo­
gutta, Ornatiline, Longilinea) participating in fermentation and acidifi­
cation of glucose and denitrifiers (Rhizobium, Rhodobacter, Aridibacter, 
Hyphomicrobium) were predominated, accounting for 42.2% of the total 
consortium for activated sludge sample and 39.8% for biofilm sample. 
Methanothrix accounting for 6.21% was widely discovered in the sludge 
bed of the reactor. As a common member of acetoclastic methanogens 
(Zinder et al., 1984), Methanothrix were suitable to be grown in the 
acetic acid environment. Moreover, lots of fermentative bacteria rapidly 
decomposed glucose into volatile fatty acid (VFA), ensuring the 
enrichment of methanogens. In contrast to methanogens, Methlogaea 
(1.53%) belonging to aerobic methanotrophic bacteria (Tarlera, 2015) 
were mainly recognized in the biofilm sample. The setting of the packing 
bed filled with small-sized sponge could delay the ascending velocity of 
the methane gas. Thus in-situ capture of the methane might be effectively 
completed by aerobic methane oxidizers to promote further conversion 
of the methane. Meanwhile, products of aerobic methane oxidation 
could be used as favorable carbon sources for nitrate denitrification. The 
large discovery of Methanothrix also confirmed this point. Detection of 
some genera (Desulfobulbus, Planctmicrobium) in both activated sludge 
and biofilm samples suggested the reduction of nitrate to ammonia 
(DNRA) pathway (Sousa et al., 2017) due to the presence of enough

dissolved methane occurred. This directly led to high accumulation of 
ammonia in the final effluent in Figs. 1c and 2. 
Fig. 2b illustrates the abundance of key functional genes involved in 
microbial metabolisms. Apparently, there was a positive correlation 
between the profiling of the functional genes and the composition of 
microbial consortium. A high relative abundance of key functional genes 
(Acs, Hdr, Fdh, Mvh) enabled to execute methane production (Sakai 
et al., 2011). Identification of key functional genes (Mmo, Ndh) verified 
the functional expression of aerobic methane oxidation (Dumont and 
Murrell, 2005). Besides, some major genes (Nir, Nor, CYP, Nos) and 
genes (Nrf, DNRA-NIR, Nit, Nis) were found to be associated with 
denitrification and DNRA, respectively (Takaya, 2002). These microbial 
results could highly imply that the co-recognition of core genera and key 
genes prompted the AMODM process for efficient removal of carbon and 
nitrogen as well as methane recovery in one-stage microaerophilic 
reactor. 
3.3. Microbial mechanism 
To deeply understand fundamental of the SMODM, the wastewater 
samples on day 118 (Phase Ⅳ) from eight-height sampling ports 
(influent, S0–S5 and effluent) in Fig.S1 were analyzed for the profile of 
COD and nitrogen along the reactor, as shown in Fig.S2. Obviously, the 
overall changing trends in COD and NO3
−-N were closely associated with 
plug-flow pattern of the EGSBBR reactor. Firstly, COD and NO3
−-N con­
centrations were fast diluted by internal recirculation. Along the reactor

height, both indicators further went down, particularly in the sludge bed 
at the reactor bottom. Based on microbial community analysis in section 
3.2, facultative fermentation and methanogenesis were responsible for 
organic removal, while nitrate was mainly reduced to nitrite and even 
ammonia there attributed by DNRA. At port S3, it was observed that 
NO2
−-N and NH4
+-N were accumulated to 24 mg/L and 8.5 mg/L, 
respectively, resulting in no obvious TN removal. As the flow upward, 
however, both nitrate and nitrite decreased in stepwise in the packing 
bed along with consistent decline of COD. As the reduction of NOx
−-N 
was performed by denitrification using products of aerobic methane 
oxidizers driven by gene Mmo in Fig. 2, AME-D distinctly took place. 
Meanwhile, NH4
+-N slightly increased to 21.5 mg/L in the final effluent, 
indicating the co-existence of DNRA and denitrification. According to 
mass balance, 73.1% COD were removed in the sludge bed, while the 
packing bed was a major zone for nitrogen removal, occupying 61.4% of 
TN removal of the whole system. Owing to the SMODM, complete COD 
and nitrate removal as well as over 80% TN removal could be achieved.

findings and removal characteristics of the reactor, possible biochemical 
reactions and standard Gibbs free energies (ΔG0’) involved in SMODM 
were proposed in the microaerophilic EGSBBR in reference to (Andalib 
et al., 2011; Conrad, R. 1999; Zhu et al., 2016):

According to above equations, the possible removal mechanism of 
the AMODM was illustrated as Fig. 3. At the bottom of the reactor, 
microaerobic condition promoted the enrichment of facultative (FHB) 
and even oxic (OHB) heterotrophic bacteria suitably grown in the sludge 
bed with high biomass, which shortly transformed glucose into low- 
molecular short-chain VFAs and then to acetic acids. After that, 
methane was likely to be produced by acetotrophic methane-producing 
bacteria (MPB) through decarboxylation of acetate. In this study, rather 
low DO (about 0.2 mg/L) not only had no adverse effects on the growth 
activity of MPB, but promoting methanogenes because of the rapid 
accumulation of VFAs through microaerobic fermentation of glucose (Fu 
et al., 2020; Montalvo et al., 2016). As the pre-aerated liquid went up­
ward in the reactor, the produced methane gas was probable to be 
captured and fixation by the biocarriers in packing bed, offering desir­
able attached-growing environment for mass proliferation of Methlogaea 
as aerobic methane oxidizers (AMOs), confirmed by microbial analysis 
in Fig. 2a. Moreover, the prolonged contact time of biomass with 
methane also favored the growth of the AMOs owing to gas mass transfer 
limitation in the packing bed. In this case, both oxygen and methane was 
consumed by AMOs, which aerobically transformed methane into 
methanol and provided alternative carbon sources for denitrifiers to 
reduce nitrate. Methanol also could be further oxidized by AMO to 
methanal (HCHO), formic acid (HCOOH) and even carbon dioxide (CO2) 
based on complete genetic pathways of aerobic methane oxidation 
depicted in Fig. 2b. Furthermore, it was observed that DNRA was a main 
pathway for nitrate reduction in both sludge and biofilm. As reported in 
previous studies (Andalib et al., 2011; Ruiz et al., 2006), it was easier for 
DNRA to occur at relatively high C/N ratio and nitrate-limiting condi­
tion, although denitrification was a competitor with DNRA for nitrate. In 
this study, as high as C/N (>10) and a relatively limited nitrate (<200 
mg/L) would favor the rapid growth of DNRA bacteria, which out­
competed denitrifiers in sludge bed under strongly low redox conditions 
(ORP < −300 mv). Additionally, the occurrence of denitrification or 
DNRA also depended on the nature of carbon source (Akunn et al., 
1993). Especially when the glucose as carbon source was available, it 
was likely to reduce nitrate via DNRA pathway. While VFAs or alcohols 
were used as carbon source, denitrification favorably occurred. These 
could also well explain the accumulation of ammonia in the effluent and 
the presence of functional genes of DNRA. As a result of large con­
sumption of glucose, denitrification driven by aerobic methane oxida­
tion (AME-D) was enhanced in methane-rich packing bed, as methanol 
replacing glucose was served as carbon source. On account of effective 
operating strategy and desirable reactor configuration, it could be 
strongly believed that the co-existence and collaboration of metha­
nogens, methanotrophs and denitrifiers was decisive to AMODM in a 
microaerophilic single system. 
4. Conclusion 
In this study, AMODM process was successfully developed in a lab- 
scale EGSBBR to make the most of the dissolved methane in-situ pro­
duced in the single methanogenic system to enhance nitrogen removal. 
The system could averagely obtain 98.8% COD and 82.7% TN removal 
efficiency as well as reduce 1/3 of the methane emission at the optimal 
C/N ratio of 16.7 using AMODM, which also recovered approximately 
23.7 mL/(L⋅d) CH4. High-throughput sequencing analysis further veri­
fied key functional bacteria and genes involved in AMODM. The reaction 
mechanism of AMODM was elucidated based on the interaction of 
methanogenic, methanotrophic, denitrifying and DNRA bacteria selec­
tively enriched in sludge and biofilm phases of the EGSBBR.
